text: The 'IKEA effect' is a cognitive bias where people value things they built themselves disproportionately more — even if the result is objectively worse.
Japanese psychologist Takahiko Masuda showed that East Asians focus on context and background in images, while Westerners focus on focal objects.
The 'rubber hand illusion' can trick your brain into feeling ownership of a fake hand in under two minutes, revealing how malleable body perception is.
People who speak multiple languages often report having slightly different personalities in each language — a phenomenon studied since the 1960s.
The concept of 'amae' in Japanese psychology describes the feeling of pleasurable dependence on another person — untranslatable in most Western languages.
Your brain processes images seen for as little as 13 milliseconds — far faster than you can consciously register seeing them.
The 'Dunning-Kruger effect' shows that people with limited knowledge in an area tend to overestimate their competence, while experts tend to underestimate theirs.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Nostalgia, once considered a medical disease in the 17th century, is now known to boost mood, increase social connectedness, and enhance meaning in life.
Forest bathing (shinrin-yoku) in Japan has been scientifically shown to lower cortisol, blood pressure, and heart rate within 15 minutes.
Stanley Milgram's 1961 obedience experiments found that 65% of participants would administer what they believed to be lethal electric shocks simply because an authority figure instructed them to.
Philip Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment had to be shut down after just 6 days when student volunteers assigned as 'guards' began psychologically abusing those assigned as 'prisoners.'
Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning experiments demonstrated that dogs could be trained to salivate at the sound of a bell alone after it was repeatedly paired with food.
The 'anchoring effect' causes people to rely heavily on the first piece of information they receive, even when that number is entirely arbitrary.
Working memory — the mental 'scratch pad' used for active thinking — can hold only about 4 chunks of information simultaneously, not 7 as once believed.
The 'bystander effect' — where individuals are less likely to help in an emergency when others are present — was first documented after the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York.
Synesthesia — a neurological phenomenon where stimulating one sense automatically evokes another — affects roughly 4% of the population, with colored letters being the most common form.
Confirmation bias leads people to search for, interpret, and remember information in a way that confirms their pre-existing beliefs, one of the most pervasive cognitive biases identified.
The 'mere exposure effect' demonstrates that simply being exposed to a stimulus repeatedly increases how much you like it — explaining why familiar songs and faces feel more appealing.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Intrinsic motivation — doing something for its own sake — is undermined when external rewards are introduced, a phenomenon known as the 'overjustification effect.'
During REM sleep, the brain is nearly as active as when awake, and emotional memories are selectively processed and consolidated — which is why you often dream about recent stressors.

The Müller-Lyer illusion — where two lines of equal length appear different due to arrow-like fins on their ends — is far less effective on the San people of the Kalahari than on Westerners, suggesting perception is culturally shaped.
Prospective memory — remembering to do something in the future — is more likely to fail when you pass through a doorway, a phenomenon researchers call the 'doorway effect.'
B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning showed that behaviors followed by rewards increase in frequency, while behaviors followed by punishment decrease — a framework still central to behavioral therapy.
The 'halo effect' occurs when a positive impression in one domain (like attractiveness) biases our evaluation of unrelated traits, such as intelligence or honesty.
People are more creative between 2–3% blood alcohol content — enough to relax prefrontal inhibitions — while complex analytical tasks require complete sobriety.
The 'peak-end rule,' discovered by Daniel Kahneman, shows that people judge an experience almost entirely by how it felt at its most intense point and at its end — not by the average.
Loss aversion — the tendency to prefer avoiding losses over acquiring equivalent gains — means losses feel roughly twice as powerful as gains of the same magnitude.
Maslow's hierarchy of needs, proposed in 1943, suggests humans are motivated by five levels of needs — from physiological survival at the base to self-actualization at the top.
Children as young as 15 months show a preference for helpful over unhelpful characters, suggesting prosocial preferences emerge before language acquisition.
The 'false memory' phenomenon was vividly demonstrated by Elizabeth Loftus, who showed that simply asking leading questions about a car accident could implant entirely false memories of broken glass.

source.name: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior

text: The Big Five personality traits — Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism (OCEAN) — are now the most widely accepted model of human personality across cultures.
Lucid dreaming — becoming aware that you are dreaming while still asleep — can be trained, and roughly 55% of people have experienced it at least once in their lives.
The 'Stroop effect' demonstrates that it takes longer to name the ink color of a word when the word spells a different color (e.g., the word RED printed in blue), revealing automatic processing.
Emotional contagion — unconsciously mimicking and synchronizing facial expressions, postures, and moods with others — is a fundamental mechanism underlying empathy.
The 'cocktail party effect' describes the brain's remarkable ability to focus on one conversation in a noisy room while still detecting your own name spoken elsewhere.
Research by Martin Seligman founding positive psychology showed that people's wellbeing depends on PERMA: Positive emotions, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment.

The Flynn Effect describes the consistent rise in average IQ scores across countries throughout the 20th century — approximately 3 points per decade — attributed to improved nutrition, education, and abstract thinking demands.

Jean Piaget's theory of cognitive development proposed that children progress through four stages — sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational — each requiring new mental structures.
The 'spotlight effect' causes people to overestimate how much others notice and remember their appearance or behavior — most people are far less focused on you than you think.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Mirror neurons — brain cells that fire both when performing an action and when observing someone else perform it — are thought to be the neural basis for imitation, empathy, and language learning.
The 'fundamental attribution error' is the tendency to over-emphasize personal character when explaining others' behavior while under-emphasizing situational factors.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The amygdala — an almond-sized brain structure — processes fear responses so quickly (within 12 milliseconds) that your body begins reacting to a threat before conscious awareness registers it.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Mental Health

text: Social comparison theory, proposed by Leon Festinger in 1954, states that people evaluate their own opinions and abilities by comparing themselves to others when objective standards are unavailable.
The Ponzo illusion — where two identical horizontal lines appear different in length when placed over converging railway-track lines — shows how the brain uses environmental context to infer depth.
Research on 'flow' states by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi found that people are happiest not during leisure, but when fully absorbed in a challenging task that matches their skill level.
The 'availability heuristic' causes people to judge the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind — making vivid or recent events seem far more probable than they are.
Attachment theory, developed by John Bowlby, proposes that infants form strong emotional bonds with caregivers that become internal models for all future relationships.
The 'spacing effect' shows that studying material in spaced intervals over time leads to dramatically better long-term retention than massed cramming — first documented by Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885.

source.name: Psychological Science in the Public Interest

text: Specific phobias affect approximately 19 million American adults, with arachnophobia (fear of spiders) and acrophobia (fear of heights) among the most prevalent.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Mental Health

text: The 'generation effect' shows that actively generating information — writing it in your own words rather than passively reading it — dramatically increases memory retention.

source.name: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior

text: Infants prefer looking at faces with direct gaze over averted gaze within hours of birth, suggesting humans are hardwired to attend to social cues from the very start of life.
The 'sunk cost fallacy' describes the tendency to continue investing in a failing project because of past unrecoverable investments — a bias that affects both financial and personal decisions.

source.name: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

text: Lev Vygotsky's 'zone of proximal development' describes the gap between what a learner can do alone versus with guidance — a concept central to modern educational scaffolding.

Prosopagnosia — the inability to recognize faces, sometimes called 'face blindness' — affects approximately 2.5% of the population and is caused by damage or atypical development of the fusiform face area.
The 'endowment effect' causes people to value objects more simply because they own them — demonstrated by studies where participants demanded far more to sell a coffee mug than they'd pay to buy it.
Research on terror management theory shows that reminders of mortality unconsciously cause people to cling more strongly to their cultural worldviews and derogate those who threaten them.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Psychological safety — the belief that one won't be punished for speaking up — is the single most important factor in high-performing teams, according to Google's Project Aristotle study.
The 'protégé effect' shows that teaching a concept to someone else, or even preparing to teach it, improves your own understanding and memory of that material significantly.

Cross-cultural studies show that the six 'basic' emotions identified by Paul Ekman — happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, anger, and surprise — are recognized from facial expressions across all studied cultures.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve shows that humans forget roughly 70% of newly learned information within 24 hours unless it is actively reviewed.
Cognitive dissonance — the discomfort felt when holding two conflicting beliefs — motivates people to reduce the inconsistency, often by changing their attitudes rather than their behavior.
Animals show clear signs of grief: elephants return to bones of deceased relatives, primates have been observed carrying deceased infants for days, and crows hold 'funerals' for fallen companions.
Sleep deprivation of 17 hours produces cognitive impairment equivalent to a blood alcohol level of 0.05%, and 24 hours of wakefulness equals 0.10% — legally drunk in most countries.
The 'framing effect' shows that presenting the same information differently (e.g., '90% survival rate' vs. '10% mortality rate') dramatically alters people's choices and risk perception.
Emotional intelligence (EQ) — the ability to perceive, manage, and use emotions — predicts job performance better than IQ in most roles, according to research by Goleman and colleagues.
The 'baader-meinhof phenomenon' (frequency illusion) occurs when you learn a new word or concept and then suddenly notice it everywhere — the brain becomes primed to detect it more readily.
Chimpanzees can pass the mirror self-recognition test — a classic test of self-awareness — from about age 4, while most human infants can do so starting around 18 months.
The 'social facilitation effect' shows that people perform well-practiced tasks better in front of others, but perform poorly on complex or novel tasks when observed.

Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences (1983) proposed that human intelligence is not a single capacity but at least eight distinct types, including linguistic, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, and naturalistic.
The 'self-serving bias' leads people to attribute their successes to internal factors (skill) and their failures to external factors (bad luck), protecting self-esteem.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Aoccdrnig to a rscheearch at Cmabrigde Uinervtisy — as this sentence demonstrates — the brain reads words as whole units using first and last letters, making scrambled middles surprisingly legible.

The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis suggests that the language you speak shapes how you think — speakers of languages with more color terms can perceptually distinguish colors faster than those with fewer terms.
Research on 'ego depletion' proposed that willpower is like a muscle that fatigues with use — later studies debate the magnitude, but decision fatigue from prolonged choice-making is well-documented.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Studies of twins raised apart show that personality traits such as conscientiousness and neuroticism are approximately 40–60% heritable, revealing a strong genetic component to character.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The phenomenon of 'inattentional blindness' was famously demonstrated by the invisible gorilla study, in which participants counting ball passes failed to notice a gorilla walking through the scene.
The 'reminiscence bump' explains why adults recall a disproportionate number of autobiographical memories from ages 15–25 — a period of identity formation when many novel 'firsts' are encoded.
Phobias acquired through conditioning can be effectively treated using systematic desensitization, a technique developed by Joseph Wolpe that gradually pairs the feared stimulus with relaxation.

The 'negativity bias' causes negative events to have a greater psychological impact than equally positive ones — humans are wired to weight threats more heavily than rewards for evolutionary survival.

Octopuses demonstrate tool use, play behavior, and individual personalities — including bold and shy types — indicating rich animal cognition in an invertebrate with a radically different brain architecture.

The 'cocktail of happiness' chemicals includes dopamine (anticipation of reward), serotonin (social status), oxytocin (bonding), and endorphins (pain relief) — each contributing differently to wellbeing.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Mental Health

text: Solomon Asch's conformity experiments showed that about 75% of participants would give an obviously wrong answer at least once to match the incorrect consensus of a group.
Body dysmorphic disorder affects about 2.4% of the population, causing people to obsessively focus on perceived — often minor or imagined — physical flaws that others typically cannot see.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Mental Health

text: The 'Tetris effect' (or 'game transfer phenomenon') occurs when playing a video game so much that its imagery and patterns intrude on waking thoughts, daydreams, and even dreams.
Carol Dweck's research on 'growth mindset' found that students who believe intelligence is malleable achieve more than those who believe it is fixed, simply because they persist through failure.
The 'cheerleader effect' is the perceptual phenomenon where people appear more attractive when seen in a group than individually, because the brain averages faces toward an idealized mean.

Harlow's controversial monkey experiments in the 1950s showed that infant rhesus monkeys preferred a soft cloth 'mother' over a wire one that provided food, demonstrating comfort contact is critical to emotional development.

The Thatcher illusion demonstrates that inverted faces are notoriously hard to process: a grotesquely altered face looks nearly normal when upside down, revealing the brain's specialized face-processing system.
Studies on 'hedonic adaptation' show that humans rapidly adjust to positive life changes — such as winning a lottery — returning to a baseline level of happiness within months.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The 'illusory correlation' bias leads people to perceive a relationship between two unrelated variables — such as associating a minority group with crime — when none actually exists.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Behavioral economist Richard Thaler's 'nudge theory' demonstrated that changing the default option in a choice architecture — such as opt-out vs. opt-in organ donation — dramatically changes population behavior.
The 'spotlight on the past' effect means people overestimate how much their future self will be defined by current emotional states — a phenomenon related to impact bias in affective forecasting.
The 'paradox of choice,' described by Barry Schwartz, proposes that having too many options leads to greater anxiety, decision paralysis, and regret — particularly in Western consumer cultures.
Blind individuals who have been sightless since birth still experience visual dreams if they lost their sight after age 5, but those blind from birth dream using their other senses instead.
The 'chameleon effect' describes automatic, unconscious mimicry of others' postures, mannerisms, and expressions — people are liked more when mimicked, even without awareness it is happening.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Grit — the combination of passion and long-term perseverance for a goal — predicts achievement in diverse settings (military, spelling bees, academics) better than IQ, according to Angela Duckworth's research.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Albert Bandura's Bobo doll experiments showed that children who watched an adult aggressively beat a doll readily imitated the behavior, demonstrating that aggression and social behaviors are learned through observation.

source.name: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

text: Aphantasia — the inability to voluntarily visualize mental images — affects roughly 2–4% of people, who cannot 'see' anything when asked to picture a beach or a loved one's face.
The 'self-reference effect' in memory means that information is better remembered when it is processed in relation to oneself — making personalized examples far more memorable than abstract facts.
Research shows that spending money on others (prosocial spending) reliably increases happiness more than spending the same amount on oneself, across diverse income levels and cultures.
The 'weapons effect' found that the mere presence of a gun in the room increased aggressive thoughts and behaviors in participants, even when the weapon was not used or mentioned.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: William James, considered the 'father of American psychology,' proposed in 1884 that emotions are the brain's interpretation of physiological changes — we are afraid because we run, not the other way around.
The 'cocktail party problem' demonstrated by Colin Cherry in 1953 was one of the first scientific demonstrations of selective attention, showing we can follow one voice while ignoring others.

source.name: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

text: Dolphins are one of only a handful of animals — along with great apes, elephants, and magpies — to pass the mirror test, suggesting a level of self-awareness previously thought exclusive to primates.

The 'hot-cold empathy gap' describes the tendency to underestimate the influence of visceral states on decision-making — people in a 'cold' rational state systematically underpredict how they'll behave when hungry, in pain, or aroused.

Cross-cultural research shows that collectivist societies (e.g., East Asian) prioritize group harmony and interdependence, while individualist societies (e.g., Western) emphasize personal autonomy — shaping cognition, behavior, and even mental health presentations.
The 'next-in-line effect' shows that people who are about to speak in a group remember very little of what the previous person said, as cognitive resources are consumed by anticipatory rehearsal.

Research on 'expressive writing' by James Pennebaker found that writing about traumatic experiences for 20 minutes over several days improves immune function, reduces depression, and enhances wellbeing.

source.name: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology

text: The 'gambler's fallacy' is the mistaken belief that past random events influence future ones — such as thinking a coin is 'due' to land heads after a streak of tails.

Curiosity activates the brain's dopamine reward system even before any information is obtained, explaining why incomplete questions feel compelling — we are neurologically driven to resolve uncertainty.
The 'Pratfall effect' shows that highly competent people become more likable after making a blunder — their mistake makes them seem more human and approachable.

Research on 'stereotype threat' by Claude Steele showed that reminding African-American students of their race before a test lowered their scores — fear of confirming a stereotype impairs performance.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Olfactory memories are among the most emotionally vivid and long-lasting because the olfactory bulb has direct connections to the amygdala and hippocampus, unlike all other senses.
The 'cocktail of love' involves three distinct brain systems — lust (sex hormones), attraction (dopamine/norepinephrine), and attachment (oxytocin/vasopressin) — which can operate independently.
The 'bizarreness effect' in memory shows that unusual and unexpected events are better remembered than ordinary ones — evolutionary pressure favored noticing anomalies.

Koko the gorilla, who learned over 1,000 signs of American Sign Language, used the language to express sadness at the death of her pet kitten — one of the most discussed animal language studies ever conducted.
The 'Matthew effect' in education describes how early reading advantages compound over time — children who read more become better readers, while those who struggle fall further behind each year.

Psychopathy is estimated to affect approximately 1% of the general population and 15–25% of prison populations, characterized by lack of empathy, shallow affect, and manipulative behavior without psychosis.
The Zeigarnik effect describes the tendency to remember interrupted or incomplete tasks better than completed ones — our brains hold open a 'mental tab' for unfinished business.
The 'decoy effect' in behavioral economics shows that introducing an irrelevant third option can dramatically shift people's choices between two existing options by reframing their relative value.
The 'Google effect' (digital amnesia) refers to the tendency to forget information that can be easily looked up online, as the brain optimizes storage for what cannot be retrieved externally.
Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) was the first cognitive-behavioral therapy, proposing that irrational beliefs — not events themselves — cause emotional disturbance.

Dreams about teeth falling out are among the most universally reported dream themes worldwide, appearing across diverse cultures with similar emotional content despite having no agreed-upon interpretation.
The 'illusory truth effect' shows that repeatedly hearing a false statement significantly increases the likelihood of believing it is true — even when warned about misinformation.
Rats display empathy: in experiments, free-roaming rats consistently opened traps to release restrained cagemates, even when food was available as an alternative reward.

The 'tip-of-the-tongue' (TOT) phenomenon occurs when you can't quite recall a word but can retrieve its first letter, number of syllables, and related words — revealing the hierarchical structure of memory.

source.name: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior

text: Carl Jung coined the concept of 'synchronicity' — meaningful coincidences that have no causal relationship but feel connected — as an attempt to explain patterns the unconscious mind notices.
Chromesthesia — a form of synesthesia where sounds trigger automatic experiences of color — has been reported by famous musicians including Franz Liszt and Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

The 'generation gap' in personality is real: longitudinal studies show each successive generation scores progressively higher on narcissism scales, though debate persists about causes and measurement.
The 'isolation effect' (von Restorff effect) predicts that an item that stands out from its surroundings — through color, size, or novelty — will be better remembered than surrounding items.
Oxytocin — the so-called 'bonding hormone' — increases trust, generosity, and in-group cooperation, but simultaneously increases suspicion and aggression toward out-group members.
Research on 'choice architecture' shows that placing healthy foods at eye level in cafeterias — without removing any options — increases their selection by 25% with no other change.
The 'sleeper effect' in persuasion describes how a message from a low-credibility source becomes more persuasive over time as the source is forgotten but the message content is retained.

Daydreaming occupies the mind for an average of 46.9% of waking hours, according to a Harvard study using experience-sampling, and a wandering mind was associated with unhappiness regardless of the activity.

The 'misattribution of arousal' experiment by Dutton and Aron found that men who crossed a scary suspension bridge were more attracted to a female researcher than those who crossed a stable bridge, confusing fear arousal with romantic attraction.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The 'contact hypothesis,' proposed by Gordon Allport, suggests that prejudice between groups decreases when they interact under conditions of equal status, shared goals, and institutional support.

Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic concept of defense mechanisms — including repression, projection, rationalization, and sublimation — remains influential in clinical psychology despite lack of empirical verification for many.
The 'planning fallacy,' identified by Kahneman and Tversky, describes the systematic tendency to underestimate task completion time even when aware that similar tasks took longer than planned.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: In the 'Good Samaritan study,' Princeton Seminary students told they were late for a lecture on the parable of the Good Samaritan walked past a slumped man in need without stopping, showing situational pressures override moral character.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The 'weapons focus effect' shows that eyewitnesses to crimes involving weapons have poorer identification of the perpetrator's face, as attention is drawn to the weapon rather than the person.

The frequency of nightmares increases during stressful life periods — combat veterans, trauma survivors, and people under chronic stress experience nightmares at dramatically higher rates than the general population.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can temporarily disrupt specific brain regions in healthy volunteers, allowing researchers to study which areas are causally necessary for functions like language, memory, and moral reasoning.
The 'what-the-hell effect' describes a pattern of disinhibition where one small transgression (breaking a diet with one cookie) leads to total abandonment of the goal (eating the whole box).

Money does increase happiness up to a point — but research by Kahneman and Deaton found that emotional wellbeing levels off around a moderate household income, while life evaluation (satisfaction) continues rising with wealth.
The 'chameleon effect' in consumer behavior shows that salespeople who mimic customers' speech patterns and body language increase purchase rates by over 20%.
Research shows that creative insights occur most often during periods of unfocused mind-wandering rather than intense concentration — supporting the idea of 'sleeping on a problem.'

The 'Barnum effect' (or Forer effect) explains why people believe vague, general personality descriptions are uniquely accurate — the same bogus 'horoscope-style' profile was accepted as personally accurate by nearly 90% of subjects.

source.name: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

text: The 'sleepwalking defense' in law is recognized in many jurisdictions because sleepwalkers are in a genuinely dissociated state — able to perform complex physical behaviors with no conscious control or awareness.
The 'recency effect' in memory means that the last items in a list are best remembered immediately after learning, while the 'primacy effect' means the first items are best remembered after a delay.
The 'social loafing effect' describes reduced individual effort when working in a group — people pull less hard in a tug-of-war when they believe others are also pulling.
Babies are born with a preference for their mother's voice, recognizing it from prenatal audio exposure — the fetal auditory system responds to external sounds from about 25 weeks gestation.
The 'scarcity heuristic' leads consumers to assign higher value to scarce items — 'limited edition' and 'only 3 left' labels reliably increase purchase likelihood even for identical products.

The 'terror of history' described by Mircea Eliade, and fear of randomness studied by psychologists, shows humans are pattern-seeking creatures who invent meaning in chaos to reduce existential anxiety.
Studies on 'awe' — the emotion triggered by vast, overwhelming stimuli — show it expands the perceived availability of time, increases prosocial behavior, and reduces inflammation markers.

The 'cruel-to-be-kind' phenomenon is a real psychological dynamic: constructive criticism from someone who clearly cares about you is psychologically easier to accept and more motivating than neutral feedback.
Mindfulness meditation, even practiced for just 8 weeks, produces measurable changes in the structure of the brain — increasing gray matter in the hippocampus and reducing amygdala reactivity.
The 'doorstep technique' (foot-in-the-door) shows that people who agree to a small initial request are significantly more likely to comply with a larger follow-up request.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Psychologists have identified 'abusive supervision' as a distinct workplace phenomenon affecting 13.6% of U.S. workers, producing psychological distress, turnover, and reduced performance across organizations.
The 'ostrich effect' in behavioral economics describes the tendency to avoid checking accounts, health results, or feedback when negative information is anticipated — literally ignoring bad news.
Babies as young as 6 months show categorical perception of phonemes from all world languages; by 12 months, this ability narrows to the sounds of their native language — a critical period closes.
The 'curse of knowledge' bias makes experts systematically overestimate how much novices understand — once you know something well, it becomes nearly impossible to imagine not knowing it.

The 'fresh start effect' shows that people are more likely to pursue goals on temporally significant dates — Mondays, the first of the month, birthdays, New Year's Day — treating them as psychological clean slates.
Laughter is contagious because hearing laughter automatically activates premotor facial regions in listeners, preparing them to join in — a form of reflexive social coordination.

The 'dark triad' of personality — narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy — while associated with negative outcomes, is also linked to higher short-term mating success and leadership attainment.
Erik Erikson's theory of psychosocial development proposed eight stages of life, each presenting a unique challenge — from 'trust vs. mistrust' in infancy to 'integrity vs. despair' in old age.
Sleep spindles — bursts of neural activity during Stage 2 sleep — play a critical role in transferring memories from the hippocampus to long-term cortical storage.
The 'simulation theory' of empathy proposes that understanding others' mental states requires internally simulating their perspective — effectively running a mental model of their experience.
The 'mere mortal effect' shows that reminding people of their mortality makes them value human connection and compassion more — death awareness can paradoxically increase kindness.

Déjà vu — the eerie sense of having experienced a new situation before — is thought to result from a brief mismatch between memory encoding and retrieval circuits, occurring in about two-thirds of the population.

Cross-cultural studies show that while the six basic facial expressions are universally recognized, the threshold for expressing them varies by culture — Japanese participants suppress negative expressions in public far more than American participants.
The 'Pinocchio effect' is real: when people lie, subtle blood-flow changes increase nasal tissue temperature, making the nose microscopically warmer — detectable via thermal imaging.

The 'WOOP' framework (Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan), developed by Gabriele Oettingen, was found to outperform pure positive visualization by incorporating mental contrasting with implementation intentions.
'State-dependent memory' shows that information learned in a particular physiological state — such as under caffeine or even underwater — is better recalled in that same state.
The 'observer effect' in psychology — where people behave differently when they know they are being observed — complicates both research design and natural behavior studies across the field.
People with depression exhibit faster forgetting of positive memories but retain negative memories at normal rates — a 'mood-congruent memory' pattern that perpetuates the disorder.
The 'identifiable victim effect' shows that people donate far more money to save a specific named individual than to statistical descriptions of thousands of unidentified victims.
Trypophobia — an aversion to clusters of small holes or bumps — affects up to 16% of people and may be an evolutionary response to patterns associated with dangerous animals and disease.

The 'false uniqueness effect' causes people to underestimate how many others share their positive attributes, while the 'false consensus effect' leads people to overestimate how many others share their beliefs.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: A classic study found that professional chess players can reconstruct a chess board from memory almost perfectly after a 5-second glance — but only for real game positions, not random piece placements.
Loneliness activates the same brain regions as physical pain, and chronic loneliness is associated with a 26% increase in the risk of premature mortality — comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

The 'cheerio test' and other object permanence tasks show that babies develop an understanding that objects exist when out of sight at around 8 months — a milestone Piaget used to map early cognitive development.
The 'contrast effect' in perception means that the same temperature water feels hotter after cold exposure and colder after hot exposure — relative context systematically shapes experience.

The 'moral licensing effect' shows that doing something virtuous gives people psychological permission to be less virtuous afterward — donating to charity can paradoxically increase subsequent selfish behavior.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The 'cognitive load theory,' developed by John Sweller, proposes that working memory has a finite capacity, and instructional designs that overload it impede learning — a principle now central to educational psychology.
The 'nocebo effect' is the harmful counterpart to placebo: negative expectations about a treatment cause real physical symptoms and worse outcomes, even with pharmacologically inert substances.

Episodic memory — the system for remembering personal experiences — is the only memory system known to involve mental 'time travel,' allowing humans to re-experience the past and pre-experience future events.

The 'grandmother cell' hypothesis proposed that single neurons encode specific complex concepts like a person's face — while mostly discredited, a 2005 study did find individual neurons in humans that fired exclusively to images of celebrities like Jennifer Aniston.
The 'Ben Franklin effect' shows that getting someone to do a small favor for you increases their liking of you — the act of helping is rationalized as evidence of affection.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Older adults display the 'positivity effect' — they selectively attend to and better remember positive stimuli over negative ones compared to younger adults, a shift theorized to reflect motivated emotional regulation as mortality becomes salient.

The 'verbal overshadowing effect' demonstrates that describing a face in words immediately after seeing it impairs subsequent recognition — linguistic encoding can interfere with the nonverbal memory system.

The 'broaden-and-build theory,' by Barbara Fredrickson, proposes that positive emotions expand awareness and encourage novel thinking, building lasting personal resources — the opposite of how negative emotions narrow focus.

The 'illusory superiority' bias (also called the Lake Wobegon effect) leads the majority of people to rate themselves above average on most positive traits — which is statistically impossible for all to do simultaneously.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Research on 'depressive realism' suggests that people with mild depression sometimes make more accurate predictions about outcomes and their own control than non-depressed individuals — though severe depression eliminates this advantage.
The 'pratfall of perfection' extends to AI and robots: research shows humans rate robots that make small mistakes as more likable and trustworthy than flawlessly perfect machines.

The 'self-determination theory' by Deci and Ryan proposes that psychological wellbeing depends on satisfying three basic needs: autonomy (feeling volitional), competence (feeling effective), and relatedness (feeling connected).
Crows use tools, plan for the future, and pass a version of Aesop's fable crow task — dropping stones into water to raise a floating food reward — showing causal reasoning in a bird.

The 'cocktail party problem' of selective hearing breaks down in noisy conditions with age — auditory attention processing declines independently of hearing acuity, explaining why elderly people struggle more in crowds.

source.name: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

text: The 'reminiscence therapy' used in dementia care leverages the robustness of early autobiographical memories — long-term memories laid down between ages 15–30 are often better preserved than recent ones in Alzheimer's disease.

The 'social brain hypothesis,' proposed by Robin Dunbar, suggests that the human neocortex evolved primarily to manage complex social relationships — and that 150 (Dunbar's number) is the cognitive limit for stable social groups.

Research on 'embodied cognition' shows that physical experiences shape abstract thought: holding a warm cup increases perceptions of social warmth, and heavier clipboards make opinions feel weightier.

The Harvard Study of Adult Development — one of the longest-running studies on happiness, spanning over 80 years — found that the quality of close relationships is the single strongest predictor of happiness and health in later life.

The 'cocktail of creativity' involves reduced activity in the default mode network's executive control regions combined with increased connectivity between the imagination network and salience network — essentially controlled chaos.

The 'marshmallow test' by Walter Mischel showed that 4-year-olds who could delay eating one marshmallow in exchange for two later had better outcomes in adolescence, though later research showed family stability is a major confound.

The 'representativeness heuristic' causes people to judge the probability of an event by how well it matches a mental prototype, leading to errors such as the 'conjunction fallacy' where specific scenarios feel more likely than general ones.

Color perception influences behavior: studies show that red increases physiological arousal and can enhance performance on detail-oriented tasks, while blue promotes creative thinking — though effect sizes vary across cultures.

The 'thin-slice judgment' phenomenon shows that people can accurately predict personality, teaching effectiveness, and even surgical malpractice risk from brief exposures of 30 seconds or less to video or audio.

Musical training in childhood produces measurable, lasting changes in brain structure — trained musicians show larger corpus callosum and motor cortex volumes than non-musicians, reflecting neural reorganization from practice.

The 'effort heuristic' leads people to judge products, art, and performances as higher quality when they believe more time and effort went into them — effort signals value independent of the actual result.
The 'placebo sleep' effect shows that telling participants they slept better than they actually did improves their cognitive performance the next day — expectation shapes actual functioning.

Research across 10 major world languages found that 'sorrow' was universally the slowest spoken emotion and 'joy' was associated with the highest pitch — suggesting some emotion-to-voice mappings are cross-culturally universal.

Clinical psychology as a formal discipline was founded by Lightner Witmer, who opened the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania in 1896 to help children with learning difficulties.

The DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), first published in 1952, has grown from 106 diagnoses to over 300 in its fifth edition, reflecting both scientific progress and cultural shifts in defining mental illness.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), developed by Aaron Beck in the 1960s, has become the most empirically validated form of psychotherapy, with hundreds of randomized controlled trials supporting its effectiveness for depression and anxiety.
Forensic psychology applies psychological science to legal questions; forensic psychologists assess defendants' competency to stand trial, sanity at the time of an offense, and risk of reoffending.

The Hare Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R), created by Robert Hare in 1980, is the gold-standard tool used by forensic psychologists to assess psychopathy; it scores 20 traits on a 0–2 scale for a maximum of 40 points.

Industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology applies psychological principles to workplace settings; the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects I-O psychology to be among the fastest-growing occupations, with demand rising as organizations prioritize employee well-being and productivity.

The Hawthorne Effect — where people improve their behavior simply because they know they are being observed — was discovered through studies at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works plant in the 1920s and 1930s.

Positive psychology, formalized by Martin Seligman in his 1998 APA presidential address, shifted the field's focus from fixing mental illness to cultivating strengths and well-being, spawning research on happiness, gratitude, and flourishing.

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's concept of 'flow' describes a state of complete absorption in a challenging activity where skills and task difficulty are perfectly matched, producing intrinsic motivation and a sense of timelessness.

Angela Duckworth's research on 'grit' — the combination of passion and perseverance for long-term goals — found it to be a stronger predictor of success than IQ in multiple domains including military training and spelling bees.

Seligman's PERMA model of well-being identifies five pillars of flourishing: Positive emotions, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment — used in positive psychology interventions worldwide.

Evolutionary psychology posits that many human behaviors — including mate preferences, kin altruism, and fear responses — are adaptations shaped by natural selection over millennia, a framework pioneered by researchers like David Buss and Leda Cosmides.

David Buss's cross-cultural study of 37 societies found consistent sex differences in mate preferences: men prioritized physical attractiveness and youth, while women prioritized resources and social status — supporting evolutionary theories of sexual selection.

Cultural psychology examines how culture and mind shape each other; landmark research by Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama showed that East Asian cultures foster interdependent self-concepts while Western cultures foster independent ones.

The WEIRD problem in psychology refers to the overrepresentation of Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic populations in research samples — a term coined by Joseph Henrich — calling into question the universality of many psychological findings.

Environmental psychology studies how physical surroundings affect human behavior and well-being; research shows that access to green spaces and natural environments reduces stress hormones and improves attention — a concept called 'restorative environments.'

Attention Restoration Theory, proposed by Rachel and Stephen Kaplan, holds that natural environments replenish directed attention capacity because they engage 'soft fascination' — effortless, involuntary attention — allowing the brain to recover from mental fatigue.

Health psychology examines how psychological factors influence physical health; the field established that chronic stress suppresses immune function, with Nobel laureate Elizabeth Blackburn linking psychological stress to accelerated telomere shortening.

source.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

text: The biopsychosocial model, introduced by George Engel in 1977, argues that health and illness arise from biological, psychological, and social factors together — replacing the purely biomedical model and now underpinning modern healthcare.

Sport psychology interventions — including visualization, goal-setting, and self-talk — can measurably improve athletic performance; the U.S. Olympic Committee has employed sport psychologists since 1978.

The concept of 'choking under pressure' in sports is linked to conscious processing theory: when athletes over-think well-practiced automated movements, performance degrades — a phenomenon studied extensively by Sian Beilock.

Music activates more areas of the brain simultaneously than almost any other stimulus; the dopamine release during 'chills' or 'frisson' from music has been quantified using PET scans, showing up to 9% increases in dopamine levels.

The Mozart Effect — the claim that listening to Mozart temporarily boosts spatial reasoning — was widely popularized after a 1993 study in Nature, but subsequent research found the effect to be short-lived and no more powerful than any other enjoyable activity.

Color psychology research shows that red increases heart rate and can elevate competitive arousal, while blue is consistently associated with calm and trust — findings that drive decisions in branding, hospital design, and sports uniforms.

A 2008 study published in Nature found that athletes wearing red in Olympic combat sports won significantly more bouts than athletes wearing blue, suggesting color can influence both the wearer's confidence and opponents' perceptions.

Groupthink, identified by Irving Janis after analyzing foreign policy disasters like the Bay of Pigs invasion, occurs when the desire for group harmony overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives, producing poor collective decisions.

Mob psychology, or crowd contagion, was first theorized by Gustave Le Bon in 'The Crowd' (1895); he observed that individuals in large groups can lose personal identity and rational thought, becoming susceptible to collective emotion and impulsive action.

Deindividuation — the loss of self-awareness and personal responsibility in group settings — was demonstrated by Philip Zimbardo's studies showing that anonymity and group membership increased antisocial behavior even in ordinary individuals.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Cult psychology research identifies a consistent pattern of recruitment: love-bombing (intense affection), isolation from outside relationships, incremental commitment escalation, and thought-stopping techniques — tactics documented in Robert Lifton's 'Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism' (1961).

Steven Hassan's BITE model categorizes cult control across four dimensions: Behavior, Information, Thought, and Emotional control — a framework used by therapists to help former cult members understand their experience.

Research on conspiracy theory belief finds that it is linked not to low intelligence but to underlying psychological needs: the need for cognitive closure, the need for uniqueness, and feelings of powerlessness or social exclusion.

The 'proportionality bias' in conspiracy thinking leads people to assume that large events must have large causes — making it psychologically difficult to accept that a lone gunman could kill a president, for example.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) was formally recognized in the DSM-III in 1980, largely driven by advocacy from Vietnam War veterans; earlier equivalent conditions had been called 'shell shock' in WWI and 'combat fatigue' in WWII.

Trauma can alter brain structure: neuroimaging studies show that PTSD is associated with a smaller hippocampus (affecting memory), reduced prefrontal cortex activity (impairing emotion regulation), and hyperreactivity of the amygdala.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), developed by Francine Shapiro in 1987, is a trauma therapy in which patients recall distressing memories while making guided eye movements; meta-analyses support its effectiveness, though the exact mechanism remains debated.

Resilience — the ability to adapt successfully in the face of adversity — is not a fixed trait but a dynamic process; longitudinal research by Emmy Werner following children in Kauai, Hawaii found that even those from high-risk backgrounds developed resilience when they had at least one supportive adult relationship.

Post-Traumatic Growth (PTG), a concept developed by Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun in the 1990s, refers to positive psychological change — including greater personal strength, new possibilities, and deepened relationships — that can emerge following a struggle with highly challenging life circumstances.

John Bowlby's attachment theory, developed in the 1950s–1980s, proposed that infants are biologically programmed to form close bonds with caregivers, and that the quality of these early bonds shapes emotional regulation and relationship patterns throughout life.

Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation experiments (1970) identified three primary infant attachment styles — secure, anxious-avoidant, and anxious-ambivalent — later expanded by Mary Main and Judith Solomon to include a fourth: disorganized attachment.

Adult attachment styles mirror infant patterns: securely attached adults are comfortable with intimacy; avoidant adults suppress attachment needs; anxious/preoccupied adults crave closeness but fear abandonment — findings from Kim Bartholomew's four-category model.

source.name: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

text: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) affects approximately 1–4% of the population and is characterized by emotional dysregulation, unstable relationships, identity disturbance, and impulsivity; it has the highest suicide attempt rate of any personality disorder at around 70–75%.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), developed by Marsha Linehan specifically for Borderline Personality Disorder, combines CBT with mindfulness and acceptance strategies; Linehan later disclosed that she herself had been diagnosed with BPD, lending personal authenticity to her approach.

Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD) is characterized by grandiosity, a need for admiration, and a lack of empathy; research suggests a 'vulnerable narcissism' subtype that is characterized by shame, hypersensitivity, and defensive self-enhancement rather than overt dominance.

The first formal IQ test was developed by Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon in France in 1905, commissioned by the French government to identify children who needed special educational assistance — not originally intended to measure innate intelligence.

The Flynn Effect — the consistent rise in average IQ scores across generations throughout the 20th century, documented by James Flynn — of roughly 3 IQ points per decade suggests that IQ measures are sensitive to environmental factors like education, nutrition, and environmental complexity.

The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), first published in 1943 by Starke Hathaway and J. C. McKinley, remains the most widely used standardized psychometric test for measuring adult psychopathology, with over 15,000 published research papers.

The Rorschach inkblot test, introduced by Swiss psychiatrist Hermann Rorschach in 1921, asks subjects to describe what they see in ten ambiguous inkblots; though controversial regarding validity, it remains used in forensic and clinical settings to assess thought patterns and personality.

The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), developed by Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan at Harvard in the 1930s, uses ambiguous images of people in social situations to elicit stories, revealing unconscious motivations and interpersonal themes.

Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, an adaptation of Binet's original test by Lewis Terman at Stanford in 1916, introduced the concept of 'intelligence quotient' (IQ) as mental age divided by chronological age times 100 — a formula now replaced by deviation IQ scores.

Learned helplessness, discovered by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier through experiments with dogs in 1967, occurs when repeated exposure to uncontrollable stressors causes animals and humans to stop trying to escape even when escape becomes possible.

Neurofeedback therapy trains individuals to consciously alter their own brain wave activity using real-time EEG feedback; research supports its use for ADHD, PTSD, and peak performance training, though debates continue about optimal protocols.

The concept of 'psychological safety,' developed by Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, describes team environments where members feel safe to take interpersonal risks; Google's Project Aristotle found it to be the strongest predictor of high-performing teams.

Terror Management Theory (TMT), derived from Ernest Becker's 'The Denial of Death,' proposes that awareness of mortality motivates people to bolster cultural worldviews and self-esteem as buffers against existential anxiety — supported by hundreds of experiments.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The Peak-End Rule, discovered by Daniel Kahneman, shows that people judge an experience largely based on how it felt at its most intense point and at its end — not the average — explaining why a procedure with a slightly longer but less painful conclusion is remembered more favorably.

Gaslighting — a form of psychological manipulation where a person causes someone to question their own reality, memory, or perceptions — takes its name from the 1944 film 'Gaslight' and is now recognized by clinicians as a pattern in abusive relationships and narcissistic abuse.

Polyvagal Theory, developed by Stephen Porges in 1994, proposes that the vagus nerve mediates three physiological states — social engagement, fight-or-flight, and freeze — and that trauma therapy can work by restoring access to the social engagement system.

source.name: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

text: The concept of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) emerged from a landmark CDC-Kaiser Permanente study (1995–1997); higher ACE scores are strongly correlated with increased risks of mental illness, addiction, heart disease, and early death.

Schema therapy, developed by Jeffrey Young in the 1980s, identifies 18 early maladaptive schemas — such as abandonment, mistrust, and emotional deprivation — that form in childhood and drive lifelong dysfunctional patterns; it is particularly effective for personality disorders.

The 'dark triad' of personality — narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy — shares a core of callousness and manipulation; research by Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams shows the triad predicts predatory social behavior and reduced empathy across cultures.

Psychedelic-assisted therapy using psilocybin is showing remarkable results in clinical trials for treatment-resistant depression; a 2021 Johns Hopkins study found that two psilocybin sessions produced rapid, large reductions in depressive symptoms lasting at least 12 months in most participants.

The Transtheoretical Model of behavior change (Prochaska and DiClemente, 1983) identifies five stages — precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance — and suggests interventions should be matched to an individual's current stage to be most effective.

The Barnum effect (also called the Forer effect), demonstrated by Bertram Forer in 1948, shows that people rate vague, general personality descriptions as highly accurate for themselves — explaining the popularity of astrology, horoscopes, and generic personality readings.

source.name: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

text: Implicit Association Tests (IAT), developed by Anthony Greenwald at the University of Washington in 1998, measure unconscious biases by timing response speed to paired concepts; they have revealed widespread implicit racial, gender, and age biases even in people who explicitly endorse egalitarian values.

Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR), developed by Jon Kabat-Zinn at UMass Medical School in 1979, has been shown in hundreds of studies to reduce anxiety, depression relapse, and chronic pain, and produces measurable changes in brain gray matter density after just 8 weeks.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), developed by Steven Hayes in the 1980s, uses mindfulness and value-clarification to increase psychological flexibility — accepting difficult thoughts and feelings rather than fighting them — and has strong evidence for anxiety disorders, depression, and chronic pain.

Self-determination theory (SDT), developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, posits that optimal motivation and well-being require satisfaction of three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness — applicable from education to healthcare to management.

The 'overjustification effect' shows that adding extrinsic rewards (like money or prizes) for an already intrinsically enjoyable activity reduces intrinsic motivation — demonstrated in classic experiments where rewarded children played less with interesting puzzles afterward.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Stereotype threat, identified by Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson in 1995, is the risk of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group; reminding Black college students of their race before an IQ test significantly lowered their scores compared to a control condition.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: The broaden-and-build theory, proposed by Barbara Fredrickson, holds that positive emotions — joy, gratitude, curiosity — broaden cognitive repertoires and build lasting personal resources (skills, relationships, resilience), whereas negative emotions narrow thinking toward immediate threats.

The Big Five personality model (OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism) is the most empirically supported personality framework, replicated cross-culturally, and predicts important life outcomes including job performance, health, and relationship quality.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Childhood adversity — poverty, abuse, neglect, parental mental illness — affects roughly 46% of U.S. children according to the American Academy of Pediatrics, making adverse childhood experiences one of the most consequential public health challenges in psychology.

Social comparison theory, introduced by Leon Festinger in 1954, holds that people evaluate their own opinions and abilities by comparing themselves to others; upward social comparisons (comparing to those better off) can motivate improvement but also reduce well-being, a dynamic amplified by social media.

The facial feedback hypothesis, supported by experiments using pen-biting to force smiling muscles, suggests that the act of making facial expressions influences emotional experience; a 2016 large-scale replication attempted to reverse earlier findings but a 2022 multi-lab study ultimately re-confirmed the basic effect.

Neuromarketing applies neuroscience and psychology tools — fMRI, EEG, eye-tracking, skin conductance — to study consumer responses; research shows that emotional brain activity, not rational deliberation, predicts purchasing behavior 80% of the time.

Seligman's work on 'explanatory style' — how people explain negative events as permanent, pervasive, and personal — predicts depression risk; an optimistic explanatory style that sees bad events as temporary and situational is linked to better health and performance.

Embodied cognition research shows that the body shapes the mind: holding a warm cup of coffee causes people to rate strangers as having warmer personalities, while physically cleaning one's hands reduces the moral residue of past misdeeds — findings that challenged the traditional brain-centric view of psychology.

The replication crisis in psychology, highlighted by the Reproducibility Project (2015), found that only 36–39% of psychology studies replicated with the same effect size and significance — prompting major reforms in preregistration, open data, and statistical practices.

Viktor Frankl's logotherapy, developed while he was a prisoner in Nazi concentration camps, holds that the primary human drive is not pleasure (Freud) or power (Adler) but the search for meaning — documented in his 1946 memoir 'Man's Search for Meaning,' which has sold over 16 million copies.

The Johari Window, created by Joseph Luft and Harry Ingham in 1955, is a four-quadrant model mapping what is known/unknown to self and others; it is widely used in IO psychology for team communication, self-awareness training, and leadership development.

Obedience research by Stanley Milgram (1963) found that 65% of ordinary participants continued administering apparently lethal electric shocks to a stranger when ordered by an authority figure — a finding that remains one of the most disturbing and debated results in the history of social psychology.

source.name: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

text: The weapons effect — a priming phenomenon — shows that the mere presence of a weapon (even in a photograph) increases aggressive thoughts and behaviors in observers, as demonstrated by Berkowitz and LePage's 1967 experiments.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Self-efficacy — the belief in one's ability to succeed in specific situations — was introduced by Albert Bandura and is among the most robust predictors of behavior and performance; it is built through mastery experiences, vicarious learning, social persuasion, and physiological states.

Emotional intelligence (EI), popularized by Daniel Goleman in 1995 after Peter Salovey and John Mayer's original 1990 framework, encompasses the ability to perceive, use, understand, manage, and regulate emotions; high EI is linked to leadership effectiveness and relationship satisfaction.

Exposure therapy, a form of CBT, is the most effective treatment for phobias and PTSD; it works by gradually and systematically presenting feared stimuli in a safe environment, enabling extinction of the conditioned fear response through a process called inhibitory learning.

source.name: Anxiety and Depression Association of America

text: Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI) is the study of how psychological processes, the nervous system, and the immune system interact; Janice Kiecolt-Glaser's research showed that married couples who argued hurtfully healed wounds 60% more slowly than those who communicated calmly.

Music therapy is a recognized clinical discipline; research shows it reduces pain perception in post-surgical patients, slows cognitive decline in dementia, and improves communication in children with autism spectrum disorder.

Locus of control, a concept developed by Julian Rotter in 1954, refers to the degree to which people believe they control outcomes in their lives (internal locus) versus ascribing control to luck, fate, or powerful others (external locus); internal locus is associated with better health and academic performance.

The Dunning-Kruger effect describes a meta-cognitive limitation where people with low competence in a domain tend to overestimate their ability, while experts tend to underestimate theirs; first demonstrated in studies of logical reasoning and grammar by David Dunning and Justin Kruger in 1999.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Sleep deprivation has profound psychological effects: after 17–19 hours without sleep, cognitive performance is equivalent to a blood alcohol level of 0.05%; sustained deprivation causes hallucinations, paranoia, and marked personality changes.

Prosocial behavior is significantly influenced by social norms: when hotels displayed signs saying most guests reuse their towels (a descriptive norm) rather than environmental appeals, towel reuse increased by 25% — demonstrating that what others do is a powerful behavioral motivator.

The amygdala hijack, a term coined by Daniel Goleman based on Joseph LeDoux's neuroscience research, describes the sudden, overwhelming emotional response — fear, rage — that bypasses the rational prefrontal cortex and is triggered when the amygdala perceives a threat, real or imagined.

The Zeigarnik effect — the tendency to remember interrupted tasks better than completed ones — was discovered by Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik in the 1920s after noticing that waiters remembered unpaid orders better than settled ones.

Psychological debriefing after traumatic events, once standard practice, has been found by systematic reviews to be ineffective and potentially harmful for preventing PTSD — illustrating the importance of evidence-based practice over clinical intuition.

Intergroup contact theory, proposed by Gordon Allport in 1954, holds that prejudice between groups decreases when members interact under conditions of equal status, common goals, cooperation, and institutional support — a foundation of desegregation policy in the United States.

Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), identified by Norman Rosenthal at the National Institute of Mental Health in 1984, affects 1–6% of the population in temperate climates; it is thought to involve disrupted circadian rhythms and serotonin deficits caused by reduced winter light exposure.

The anchoring bias leads people to rely heavily on the first piece of information encountered (the anchor) when making decisions; in one study, real estate agents given houses with high listed prices gave higher independent valuations — showing the effect extends beyond naive judgments.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Emotional contagion — the process by which emotions spread between people through mimicry and physiological synchrony — operates automatically and below conscious awareness; research shows that 70 seconds of exposure to another person's emotion significantly influences one's own mood.

William James and Carl Lange independently proposed in 1884–1885 that emotions are our perception of physiological changes — we are afraid because we run, not the reverse — a theory still debated and refined in modern affective neuroscience.

Psychological first aid (PFA), endorsed by the WHO and Red Cross, is a research-informed approach to support people in the immediate aftermath of a disaster; unlike debriefing, PFA focuses on practical support, safety, and social connection rather than encouraging trauma narrative.

Moral disengagement, a concept developed by Albert Bandura, describes cognitive mechanisms — displacement of responsibility, dehumanization, moral justification — through which ordinarily moral people can commit harmful acts by disabling their moral self-regulatory processes.

The frustration-aggression hypothesis, proposed by Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer, and Sears in 1939, holds that aggression is always the result of frustration — a claim later refined by Berkowitz to state that frustration produces a readiness to aggress, not aggression itself.

Operant conditioning, developed by B.F. Skinner, uses reinforcement and punishment to shape behavior; variable-ratio reinforcement schedules — where rewards come after an unpredictable number of responses — produce the highest and most persistent rates of behavior, explaining the addictive pull of slot machines.

Classical conditioning, discovered by Ivan Pavlov through salivating dogs, forms the basis of many anxiety disorders: neutral stimuli paired with aversive events acquire the power to trigger fear responses — the mechanism behind phobias and PTSD triggers.

Observational learning (social learning), demonstrated by Albert Bandura's Bobo doll experiments (1961), showed that children imitate aggressive behavior seen in adults even without direct reinforcement — challenging purely behaviorist accounts of learning.

source.name: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

text: The concept of 'ego depletion,' proposed by Roy Baumeister, suggested that willpower is a limited resource that gets used up like a muscle — a compelling idea now disputed by large replication failures, illustrating psychology's ongoing self-correction.

Type A behavior pattern — characterized by competitiveness, time urgency, and hostility — was linked to coronary heart disease by cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman in the 1950s; subsequent research identified hostility as the most toxic component.

source.name: Journal of the American Medical Association

text: Hardiness, a concept developed by Salvatore Maddi and Suzanne Kobasa from research on Illinois Bell executives during a massive corporate upheaval, describes a protective personality constellation of commitment, control, and challenge that buffers against stress-related illness.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Humor has measurable psychological and health benefits: laughter increases pain tolerance, reduces stress hormones like cortisol, boosts immune function, and strengthens social bonds — Robert Provine's research showed 30% of laughter occurs during humor but 70% is social bonding.

The placebo effect extends well beyond pain: placebos produce measurable neurochemical changes including endorphin release, and open-label placebo studies (where patients know they're taking a sugar pill) still produce significant therapeutic effects, particularly in IBS.

Loneliness is as dangerous to health as smoking 15 cigarettes per day, according to a meta-analysis by Julianne Holt-Lunstad; it increases mortality risk by 26%, making social isolation a recognized public health crisis.

The 'pratfall effect,' identified by Elliot Aronson in 1966, shows that a highly competent person who makes a blunder becomes more likable — not less — because the mistake makes them seem more human and approachable.

The mere threat of social exclusion changes behavior: even reminders of ostracism cause people to become more conformist, more likely to imitate others, and more motivated to rebuild social connections — findings from Kipling Williams' Cyberball exclusion paradigm.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Cognitive dissonance, Leon Festinger's 1957 theory, holds that inconsistency between beliefs or between beliefs and actions creates psychological discomfort that people are motivated to reduce — often by changing the belief rather than the behavior.

Persuasion research by Robert Cialdini identified six principles of influence: reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, and scarcity — documented in his 1984 book 'Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion,' which has sold over 5 million copies.

The foot-in-the-door technique, studied by Freedman and Fraser in 1966, shows that agreeing to a small initial request dramatically increases compliance with a larger subsequent request — because people seek consistency between their self-image and their behavior.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Narrative transportation — deep absorption in a story — is a powerful mechanism of attitude change; people who become transported into a fictional narrative update their real-world beliefs in the direction of the story, even when they know the story is fiction.

Oxytocin, dubbed the 'love hormone,' promotes trust, bonding, and generosity — but it also intensifies in-group favoritism and out-group hostility, revealing a dual nature that researchers now describe as promoting 'tend-and-defend' rather than universal compassion.

source.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

text: The concept of 'psychological reactance,' developed by Jack Brehm in 1966, holds that when people feel their freedom is threatened, they become motivated to restore it — explaining why banning something often increases its desirability (the forbidden fruit effect).

Humor styles differ in their psychological impact: affiliative and self-enhancing humor correlate with well-being and resilience, while aggressive and self-defeating humor correlate with neuroticism and poorer mental health — a distinction developed by Rod Martin's Humor Styles Questionnaire.

Cognitive load theory, developed by John Sweller in 1988, holds that working memory has a limited capacity, and instructional design must manage intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load to optimize learning — the basis of principles like split-attention effect and worked examples.

The spacing effect — the finding that distributed practice over time yields better long-term memory than massed practice (cramming) — was first described by Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885 and remains one of the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology.

source.name: Psychological Science in the Public Interest

text: The testing effect (retrieval practice) demonstrates that recalling information from memory strengthens retention far more than re-reading the same material; this principle underpins the use of flashcards, practice tests, and spaced retrieval in modern educational design.

Stereotype content model, developed by Susan Fiske, shows that social groups are evaluated on two dimensions — warmth and competence; this 2x2 framework predicts that groups seen as low-warmth/high-competence (like rich people) elicit envy, while low-warmth/low-competence groups elicit contempt.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Affective forecasting errors — people's tendency to mis-predict the duration and intensity of their future emotional states — were documented by Timothy Wilson and Daniel Gilbert; people systematically overestimate how bad they'll feel after negative events, a bias called 'impact bias.'

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Psychological immune system — described by Daniel Gilbert — refers to unconscious cognitive processes that help people adapt to and rationalize negative life events; it explains why people often feel better after misfortune than they predicted, as they construct meaning and find silver linings.

Need for cognition, a dimension of individual difference in which some people enjoy effortful thinking and others prefer heuristics, predicts resistance to misinformation; high-need-for-cognition individuals seek out complex information and are less likely to rely on cognitive shortcuts.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Evolutionary psychological research on fear reveals that humans have prepared learning for ancestral threats (snakes, spiders, heights) and acquire these fears more quickly and extinguish them more slowly than fears of modern dangers like cars and electrical outlets.

The gender paradox of well-being shows that while women report higher rates of depression and anxiety than men, they also report higher levels of positive emotion and life satisfaction — a paradox explained partly by women's greater emotional expressivity and access to social support.

Eudaimonia — flourishing through living meaningfully and exercising one's potential — is distinguished from hedonia (pleasure-seeking) in positive psychology; research by Carol Ryff identifies six components of eudaimonic well-being: autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations, purpose in life, and self-acceptance.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

text: Moral psychology research by Jonathan Haidt proposes the Social Intuitionist Model: people make moral judgments quickly and intuitively, and only then construct post-hoc reasoning to justify them — inverting the rationalist assumption that reason drives moral decisions.

The actor-observer bias leads people to attribute their own behavior to situational factors while attributing others' behavior to their character — the flip side of the fundamental attribution error, together demonstrating a pervasive self-serving asymmetry in social perception.

The just-world hypothesis, identified by Melvin Lerner in 1965, is the tendency to believe that people get what they deserve — a cognitive bias that leads to victim-blaming and reduces charitable impulses toward those who suffer undeservedly.

source.name: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
